title: Taking Charge Is Not About Getting Your Way
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece distinguishes leaders who take charge because a situation genuinely requires it from leaders who need to take charge because they can't tolerate not being in control. The former is described as an act of leadership; the latter as an act of control and dominance disguised as decisiveness. The author offers a simple diagnostic for telling the two apart: how comfortable a leader is following someone else's plan rather than always directing the action. Great leaders, the piece argues, are also great followers, and that dual comfort with leading and following is what actually earns team trust. It closes with a direct challenge to readers to examine their own record as a follower, not just as a leader.
points: Taking charge out of necessity is leadership; taking charge out of a need for control is dominance.
Leaders with a controlling nature struggle to delegate and prefer their own strategies every time.
The best diagnostic is how comfortable a leader is following someone else's plan.
Great leaders demonstrate strong followership, which is what actually builds trust with the team.
quotes: Those who must take charge falsely believe that without them things won’t happen.
Taking charge when the situation calls for it is very different from the need to get your own way.
Leaders who have a deep-seated need to control situations and take charge are uncomfortable not directing action.
So how does a leader with a bias for action know whether they are actually leading or simply controlling by nature? The answer lies in how they follow.
Great leaders are also great followers. They don’t always need to be in charge or direct the action.
